content: Okay so it is now April 3 and I want to do a proper debrief on the April 1 price revision at Osteria Morishita while the reactions are still fresh in my head. It has been three full dinner services since the changes went live and I have been watching very closely — both the customer reactions at the table and the review situation online. The headline is that things went better than I feared, but I also made a simultaneous supply chain change that I want to think through carefully with you, because I find myself carrying more uncertainty about that side than I expected to be carrying. I thought the pricing changes would be the nerve-wracking part, and it turned out to be the opposite.

Three days across multiple dinner services is a genuinely useful early window for reading how a price revision has landed. You get enough repetition to distinguish a pattern from a fluke, but the reactions are still fresh and the emotional charge around the changes has not yet settled into background noise. The fact that you expected the pricing to be the nerve-wracking part and it turned out not to be is interesting — that inversion is worth examining. It suggests either that the pricing was better calibrated than you worried, or that the supply chain change surfaced a risk you had not fully mapped when you were making the decision. Walk me through both sides in whatever order makes sense to you. What was the structure of the April 1 revision on the menu price side?

The anchor for the whole revision was the dinner average ticket. The target I had been modeling toward since February was 9,200 yen — that is the number I needed the dinner average to reach in order to get our gross margin back to roughly where it was in 2024 before input costs started compressing everything. Before the revision, we were running around 8,400 yen on the dinner average, which felt thin relative to where protein costs and imported ingredient costs have been moving since late last year. The 9,200 yen target is meaningful but not aggressive by Higashi-Azabu standards. The neighborhood has absorbed a lot of repricing over the past two years and the guest base at our level of the market is not primarily optimizing on price per dish the way a more casual segment would be.

On the individual item level, the most consequential single change was the tagliatelle al ragu bolognese. I raised it from 2,400 to 2,700 yen. That dish carries the identity of the restaurant more than anything else on the menu. It is the dish in every Tabelog review, it is what regulars recommend to friends who become regulars themselves, it is what I think of when I think about what Osteria Morishita is. I deliberated over that price move longer than any other single decision in the revision. A 300 yen jump on the most visible dish is the kind of thing that can either land without comment or become the specific number someone mentions in a review.

On the lunch side, we run set courses rather than a la carte at midday, so the revision there was cleaner. The 2-course was raised to 2,000 yen and the 3-course was raised to 2,600 yen. Those were the primary structural moves. There were a few adjustments on the secondi — the branzino and the agnello — but those are less exposed in terms of customer memory and review culture.

The logic of anchoring to a dinner average ticket target of 9,200 yen rather than designing around individual item increases is the right way to think about a revision of this kind. The average ticket is the actual economic variable. Individual dish prices are the levers, but the lever positions only matter insofar as they produce the right ordering behavior in aggregate — dessert attachment, wine by bottle versus glass, whether guests take both a pasta and a secondi. If you set the item prices correctly but the menu does not organically produce depth of ordering, the average ticket will land below the 9,200 yen target regardless of the sticker prices.

The tagliatelle al ragu bolognese move from 2,400 to 2,700 yen is a 12.5 percent increase on your anchor dish. The psychological risk is well-known: when a price on a ritualized item crosses a threshold that was previously taken for granted, it can interrupt the unconscious re-ordering pattern and force a deliberate recalculation. Whether that recalculation ends in reorder or substitution depends on how deeply the ritual is embedded. You said regulars recommend this dish to friends who become regulars — that level of identity attachment generally insulates against substitution behavior even at a meaningful price increase. The question is how it actually played out across the three services.

On lunch: raising the 2-course to 2,000 yen and the 3-course to 2,600 yen in a set-course format is structurally different from a la carte repricing. Set course guests are making one total-value judgment rather than doing iterative arithmetic across the menu. What was the competitive benchmark for those lunch prices in the neighborhood?

Before I locked in the lunch numbers, I did a manual comparison across five other trattorias and osterie within about ten minutes of 3-14-7 Higashi-Azabu. The 2-course at 2,000 yen and the 3-course at 2,600 yen landed right in the middle of the local range — we were not the most expensive, we were not the least expensive. That matters because the guest who comes in for a weekday lunch is not comparing us to our own old menu. They are comparing us to every other lunch they have had in the neighborhood recently. If we are priced within the normal range of what the area offers at our quality level, the price does not register as a departure from expectation. The risk with being a first mover on a price increase is that you become the outlier reference point and the outlier reads as expensive. By staying inside the local competitive range, we neutralized that risk.

I also took care with the team preparation. We had a full staff meeting on the evening of March 31, the night before the April 1 revision went live. I walked everyone through the rationale — ingredient costs have moved significantly over the past eighteen months, we have maintained sourcing and preparation standards throughout, and the new prices reflect where the market and the cost structure actually are. The message I gave the front-of-house staff was that if a guest asks about the prices, they should be able to have that conversation directly and without defensiveness. The reasoning is straightforward and they do not need to apologize for it.

The competitive benchmarking is doing important protective work. The reference frame for a price judgment is almost never the restaurant's own previous menu — it is the immediate alternatives in the guest's consideration set. If Osteria Morishita's 2-course at 2,000 yen and 3-course at 2,600 yen fall in the middle of the neighborhood range, you have effectively made the revision invisible from a market positioning standpoint. The guest who might otherwise register a price change as a signal of inflation is instead confirming that you are priced normally for what you offer.

The staff preparation on March 31 is worth noting as a process decision. Price revisions fail at the table far more often from poor service execution than from the prices themselves. When a server is uncertain, slightly apologetic, or volunteering information in a way that draws attention to the change, it signals discomfort to the guest and the guest mirrors that discomfort back as complaint. Briefing the team with a clear rationale and a non-defensive posture shifts the table interaction from potential awkwardness into a routine menu conversation. The fact that you did that the night before rather than a week before is also sensible — the message is fresher and the team is less likely to have accumulated secondary anxiety about it.

Now tell me how the three dinner services actually went. What was the customer reaction, and what does the early ticket data look like?

The customer reaction was genuinely much better than I was prepared for. The most honest summary I can give you is: minimal pushback. That is what I keep coming back to when I think about the three services since April 1. Some regulars glanced at the menu, noticed that the tagliatelle al ragu bolognese was now at 2,700 yen rather than where it had been, and made a brief comment — something like 'oh, the bolognese has gone up a bit' — and then ordered it. Nobody substituted to a cheaper pasta. Nobody made it a point of escalation. Nobody brought it up again on the way out. In maybe three days of service, I can count the tables who mentioned the prices at all on one hand, and in every case it was a passing observation, not a grievance.

The metric I was watching most carefully was the review situation, because that is the fastest external signal of unhappy customers. A guest who feels overcharged tends to write about it quickly, while the emotion is still fresh. I have been checking Tabelog and Google every morning since the April 1 revision went live. No review impact — the scores have not moved, and I have not seen any new review that even mentions price. Three days of stable scores is meaningful given the specific complaint behavior of guests who feel wronged by a restaurant price change.

On the ticket data: we had modest midweek covers, nine on Wednesday and twelve on Thursday. But the dinner average ticket across those two nights ran between 9,100 and 9,400 yen, which brackets the 9,200 yen target closely. More importantly the ordering pattern was what I needed to see — secondi are being taken, we are selling bottles rather than glasses at a good ratio, dessert attachment is solid. The menu architecture is producing the ordering depth the target requires.

Minimal pushback and no review impact after three full dinner services since April 1 is a genuinely strong early result, not just an absence of bad news. The psychology of complaint behavior makes the no review impact finding more significant than it might sound in isolation. Guests who feel overcharged are motivated complainers — the feeling of having paid more than something was worth is an active irritant, and Tabelog and Google give that irritation a constructive outlet that is immediately available. The guest who had a wonderful evening thinks about writing a review when they have leisure time three days later. The guest who felt wronged reaches for their phone in the taxi home. The absence of any new reviews mentioning price across those three services means the guests who experienced the new prices at Osteria Morishita did not leave with that particular grievance activated.

The ticket data is encouraging within the context of what midweek covers look like. Nine and twelve covers are not a Friday or Saturday sample, and the guests at midweek dinner at an osteria in Higashi-Azabu tend to skew toward regulars and neighborhood loyalists rather than occasion diners. If anything, those guests are more likely to notice a price change than a Saturday reservation party. The fact that the average ticket ran 9,100 to 9,400 yen in that population and the ordering depth held suggests the revision is working at the level where the risk of price sensitivity is highest.

Friday will be a more demanding test — fuller house, more first-timers or less frequent visitors, more people making a price-to-expectation judgment on less prior goodwill. What are you expecting from this weekend, and what would you need to see to feel confident the 9,200 yen dinner average is structurally achievable, not just a midweek sample artifact?

I want to see Friday and Saturday sustain the 9,100 to 9,400 range on full or near-full covers. If the midweek numbers held in a lower-pressure environment, a weekend with more covers should, if anything, be more favorable — occasion diners spend more freely than regulars who are thinking about their weekly rhythm with us. The variable I would be watching is whether the secondi attachment rate holds. If weekend guests are more likely to skip the secondi and build a lighter meal of antipasto plus pasta, the average ticket drops and the revision has to be interrogating why that is happening. But I do not have data for that yet.

What I want to shift to now is the supply side, because that is where my residual anxiety lives. The olive oil situation is what is actually keeping me up a little at night, and I think I made a good decision but I want to stress-test it.

The secondi attachment rate is exactly the right metric to watch as a leading indicator of whether the menu is functioning as designed. If weekend guests are skimming the lighter path through the menu, it tells you something about how the menu reads in the higher-stakes, less-habituated booking — are guests in a celebrating mode that drives depth of ordering, or a more cautious mode that drives single-course comfort choices. You will have a clearer read by Sunday.

On the supply side: walk me through the olive oil situation from the beginning. What changed, what was the rationale, and what specifically is producing the residual anxiety?

The situation is this. Our olive oil had been sourced through Solleone Japan — they are our primary importer for Italian specialty products, the relationship goes back several years, very reliable. Within the Solleone Japan relationship, the specific product we had been buying was the Frantoio Franci brand. Frantoio Franci is a Tuscan producer, well-regarded, their IGP Toscano line is a solid and consistent extra virgin. Good oil. We made the decision to switch from Frantoio Franci to a less expensive blend that Solleone carries under their own house label. The cost saving on olive oil by making that switch is 22% on what we were spending. Given the volume of olive oil that goes through a functioning Italian restaurant kitchen across a full year — cooking base, finishing, the bread service at dinner — that 22% represents real money.

The rationale at the time I made the decision was sound: the Solleone house blend is decent oil, the supply relationship stays intact, and most of the olive oil use in the kitchen is in applications where nobody would ever detect the difference between a good finishing oil and a workhorse blend. That rationale is still correct. But I think I underweighted where the oil actually reaches the guest in a form where they can taste it without the cooking masking everything.

The 22% saving on olive oil cost is significant given the role olive oil plays across a full Italian kitchen operation. The important thing to do is map every application in the kitchen by the degree of sensory exposure to the guest — meaning how much of the oil character actually reaches someone sitting at the table in a perceptible form.

At one end of the spectrum are the cooking applications: the soffritto base for a ragu or braise, the saute work, the pasta preparation, anything where the oil is heated to temperatures that volatilize the aromatic compounds that distinguish a premium producer oil from a competent blend. In those applications, the Solleone house blend will perform identically to Frantoio Franci for any purpose that matters to a guest's experience. The character of the original oil is simply not present in the finished dish in any detectable way. That is probably 70 to 80 percent of the volume in a kitchen like yours.

At the other end are the raw or barely-heated applications where the oil is effectively the star of what is in front of the guest — a finishing drizzle at the pass over a cooked dish, a tableside presentation where the oil arrives in a small vessel and gets applied by the guest or the server, or a bread service where the oil is offered on its own with nothing but bread and salt to frame it. In those applications, the character of the oil is exactly what you are serving. What does Osteria Morishita's exposure in that second category look like?

The exposure is real and I had not mapped it clearly enough before I committed to the switch. Let me be specific. The cooking applications — soffritto bases for the ragu, the pasta work, the saute for the secondi — that is probably 75 to 80 percent of the oil we use. In those contexts the Solleone blend is perfectly adequate and I stand by the switch completely. The remaining 20 to 25 percent is where the problem lives.

We do a bread service at dinner, before the first course arrives. Good bread, sea salt, and a small pour of olive oil. That service is the most naked presentation of the oil we have anywhere in the restaurant. No heat, no aromatics, no sauce to integrate with. The oil is what the guest is tasting. And it is the first thing that comes out of the kitchen. Before they have tasted the antipasto, before the tagliatelle al ragu bolognese arrives, before they have any context for the evening's cooking — the bread and oil is the first impression the kitchen makes. We also finish the agnello and the spring branzino with a drizzle at the pass. That is less volume than the bread service, but it is similarly exposed because it is raw oil on a plated dish being tasted directly.

I did a side-by-side tasting of the Solleone house blend against the Frantoio Franci in a few applications after the fact, and the result was more or less what you would predict. In the cooked applications, the difference is not detectable. In the bread service context, the Frantoio Franci is noticeably cleaner and more expressive — there is a peppery finish that is characteristic of good Tuscan extra virgin that the Solleone blend does not have at the same level. A guest who eats thoughtfully will not necessarily identify the absence as a downgrade, but they may have a subtly less satisfying impression of the bread course and not know why.

The bread service as the first-impression problem is important to take seriously. The mechanism is not just about whether the oil is good or not good on its own terms — it is about what that first course does to the guest's expectation frame for the rest of the evening. If a guest sits down at Osteria Morishita, picks up a piece of bread, dips it in olive oil, and has a genuinely compelling moment — that peppery Tuscan finish, the clean fat, the sense that something attentive happened here — they carry a positive prior into the antipasto, into the tagliatelle al ragu bolognese, into everything that follows. The kitchen gets the benefit of the doubt. If the bread course is neutral, the prior is neutral, and the kitchen has to build that positive impression from the antipasto forward without the running start.

The practical path is clear, and it does not require you to abandon the 22% saving wholesale. Use the Solleone house blend for all cooking applications — the full 75 to 80 percent of your volume where the switch is invisible to any guest. Maintain a smaller, separate purchase of the Frantoio Franci or another quality finishing oil only for the bread service and the pass drizzle. You are protecting roughly 20 to 25 percent of the volume, so the net olive oil cost saving moves from the full 22% to something in the 15 to 17 percent range depending on the price differential. That is still a meaningful annual saving, and you are not trading it for a degraded first impression. The two-product approach also gives you supply resilience: you have already validated the Solleone blend across the applications that matter most by volume, so if there is ever a shortage or a price move on your finishing oil, you have options. What is your read on the operational complexity of running two olive oil products in the kitchen simultaneously?

I went back and forth on the two-product question for a while before the switch, actually. My initial hesitation was that adding a second SKU means more to track, more potential for the kitchen team to reach for the wrong container under pressure during a busy service, more cognitive load on what should be a simple supply chain. But I think I was overcomplicating it. In practice it is two clearly labeled containers in the same storage location they always lived. A brief conversation with the kitchen team — this one for cooking, this one for bread service and finishing — and within a week it is just the new normal. It is not meaningfully more complex than having both a table salt and a finishing salt, which we already do without anyone confusing them.

I think the concern about complexity was actually a displacement of a different anxiety, which was that by running two products I was implicitly admitting that the switch had not been as clean as I had presented it to myself when I made the decision. Once I separated the olive oil question from that ego concern, the two-product solution was obviously right. We are going to implement it before the weekend service. I have already called Solleone Japan and confirmed we can keep a small monthly allocation of the Frantoio Franci line alongside the house blend order. The account manager was not at all surprised — apparently we are not the first account to ask for that arrangement in the past couple of months.

The displacement dynamic you identified is worth naming explicitly, because it shows up frequently in operational decisions and is harder to catch in the moment than in retrospect. When a decision has some ambiguity in it — in this case, a supply switch that was mostly right but had a real gap in one area — there is a pull toward resolving the ambiguity by declaring the decision clean rather than complicating it by partially revising course. The ego logic is that the two-product solution reads as 'I got it wrong,' when the correct read is 'I solved 80 percent of the problem correctly and now I am fixing the remaining 20 percent.' Those are very different things. The fact that you caught it after three days and are implementing before the weekend service is exactly the right speed of response.

The Solleone account manager's reaction is also telling. When she says you are not the first account to ask for that arrangement, she is confirming that the tiered-use approach — house blend for cooking, premium finishing oil for tableside applications — has become a standard solution in the restaurant segment for navigating the current import cost environment. You arrived at it independently, which means the reasoning was sound, and the fact that it is a common solution in the peer group means there is no positioning cost to it. Your kitchen will run the same way a lot of well-run Italian restaurants in Tokyo are running right now.

Stepping back to look at the April 1 revision as a whole: you moved the dinner average ticket toward a target of 9,200 yen, the early midweek data brackets that target, you have minimal pushback and no review impact after three dinner services, the lunch restructure with the 2-course at 2,000 yen and the 3-course at 2,600 yen landed without friction, and you are closing the one real gap in the olive oil switch before the weekend. That is a coherent set of moves that are landing well. What is the remaining area of uncertainty you are carrying going into Friday and Saturday?

Honestly the remaining uncertainty is mostly the weekend data. Midweek is a sample I trust in terms of signal quality but not in terms of cover volume. Friday and Saturday will be full houses or close to it, and the guest profile shifts — more occasion diners, some first-timers who found us on Tabelog, some larger tables who booked for a birthday or an anniversary. Those guests are spending in a different mode than a regular who comes in on a Tuesday for a quiet dinner and the tagliatelle al ragu bolognese. The occasional diner is more likely to order freely across the menu, which is good for the average ticket, but they are also doing a fresh value assessment because they do not have accumulated trust in the restaurant. If the tagliatelle al ragu bolognese at 2,700 yen does not feel worth it to someone experiencing it for the first time alongside a competing mental price anchor of what pasta costs elsewhere, that is where a review gets written.

I think the setup is as good as I can make it. The food quality has not changed. The service briefing was done properly. The pricing is within the neighborhood range on dinner and comfortably within range on lunch. The olive oil situation will be corrected before Friday. I just have to let the weekend happen and see what the data shows. I will know a lot more by Sunday.

The frame you have right now is the correct one, and it is worth being specific about why. You have done everything that is within your control to do before Friday. The food quality is maintained. The team is briefed with a confident, non-defensive posture. The prices are calibrated against the neighborhood competitive set. The olive oil correction addresses the one identifiable guest-facing gap before the higher-stakes service. What happens this weekend is data, not judgment on the quality of the preparation.

The concern about first-timers and the tagliatelle al ragu bolognese at 2,700 yen is worth holding with some proportion. A first-time guest at Osteria Morishita in Higashi-Azabu is not typically walking in with a 1,800 yen pasta expectation. The neighborhood positioning, the restaurant's Tabelog profile, the context of the booking all pre-set an expectation range before anyone looks at a menu. If someone arrives at a dinner reservation at your restaurant expecting commodity pasta pricing, there is a mismatch in the reservation decision that precedes the menu interaction, and the tagliatelle al ragu bolognese at 2,700 yen is not the cause of their dissatisfaction. For guests who arrived with expectations calibrated to the actual positioning of the restaurant, 2,700 yen for a hand-made pasta with a slow-cooked ragu bolognese at this level in this neighborhood is not an outlying number.

The more meaningful weekend metric than the first-timer reaction is what the Saturday evening data shows about ordering depth. If a full house on Saturday averages 9,200 yen or above with normal secondi attachment and wine sales, the April 1 revision is structurally working. By Sunday you will have that number. Everything you have done in the past week has set up the best possible conditions for that result. Now the restaurant just has to run.
